title: RamanBench: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Machine Learning on Raman Spectroscopy
claim: Our benchmark occupies a distinct data regime that existing benchmarks miss, and a long-standing baseline stayed state-of-the-art until recently.
layout: 2 panels side by side, scatter left, step-line timeline right, shared color legend
description: Two plots sit side by side. Panel (a), "Samples vs Features", is a log-log scatter of number of samples against number of features. Orange squares (TALENT) and yellow triangles (TabArena) cluster at the upper left, where there are many samples and few features. Blue diamonds (UCR) and light-blue plus signs (UEA) fall in the middle. Pink circles (RamanBench) sit toward the lower right, in the high-feature, low-sample region. A dotted vertical line marks 100 features. A legend below the plots gives each collection's dataset count. Panel (b), "Model Progress over Time", plots Elo against release year with a broken x-axis. A grey step line connects labeled state-of-the-art models: Logistic Reg., Extra Trees, CatBoost, ROCKET, TabPFN v2 and TabPFN v2.5. PLS is shown as a hollow circle near 1000 Elo, and faded dots mark other models. The eye goes first to the pink points in (a) and the steep orange rise at the top right of (b).
caption: RamanBench: High dimensional, low sample ML. Left: Sample count vs. feature count for RamanBench (pink) and four reference benchmark collections; RamanBench occupies a distinct high-dimensional, low-sample regime. TabArena [9] and TALENT [10]: tabular ML; UCR [11] and UEA [12]: Time Series Classification (TSC). Right: Model performance (Elo) vs. release year. RamanBench enables a retrospective view: Partial Least Squares (PLS), the long-standing domain standard, would have been State-of-the-Art (SOTA) for most of the past decades; only recently have modern methods begun to clearly surpass it, with the SOTA frontier still advancing.
abstract: Machine learning (ML) has transformed many scientific fields, yet key applications still lack standardized benchmarks. Raman spectroscopy, a widely used technique for non-invasive molecular analysis, is one such field where progress is limited by fragmented datasets, inconsistent evaluation, and models that fail to capture the structure of spectral data. We introduce RamanBench, the first large-scale, fully reproducible benchmark for ML on Raman spectroscopy, consisting of streamlined data access (https://pypi.org/project/raman-data/), evaluation protocols and code (https://pypi.org/project/raman-bench/), as well as a live leaderboard (https://huggingface.co/spaces/HTW-KI-Werkstatt/RamanBench). It unifies 77 datasets (including 17 first released with this benchmark) across four domains, comprising 325,862 spectra and spanning classification and regression tasks under diverse experimental conditions. We benchmark 28 models under a standardized protocol, including classical methods (e.g., PLS), Raman-specific (e.g., RamanNet), tabular foundation models (TFMs; e.g., TabPFN), and time-series approaches (e.g., ROCKET). TFMs consistently outperform domain-specific and gradient boosting baselines, while time-series models remain competitive. However, no single method dominates across these heterogeneous datasets, revealing that Raman spectroscopy remains an open challenge for machine learning. Therefore, we invite the community to contribute new approaches to our living benchmark, with the potential to accelerate advances in critical applications such as medical diagnostics, biological research, and materials science.
